mainTopic: Rain for an individual, signs of rain, and the argument between רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע about where rain comes from
overview: The amud opens by finishing two stories about רב פפא and students who caused him pain. After a frightening dream, he parts from three Rabbis with a hint of final farewell. Later, רב שימי בר אשי goes silent once he sees how his challenges embarrass his teacher. The גמרא then returns to rain. Using a פסוק in זכריה and a ברייתא, it shows that rain can fall for one person, one field, and even one plant, and it tells the story of רב דניאל בר קטינא's garden. It explains the word חזיזים as flying clouds that signal rain, and gives signs from drizzle along with two stories about עולא's visit to בבל. Finally, רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע argue whether rain comes from the ocean below or from the waters above. The גמרא matches פסוקים to each view, and רבי יהושע's answer about the 'storehouses' פסוק continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רב פפא's dream about the three shepherds
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא hears a פסוק in his dream about cutting off three shepherds. The next day he says goodbye to the three Rabbis with a hint that this is their final parting.
steps.simpleTranslation: In his dream they read to רב פפא the פסוק: 'And I cut off the three shepherds.' The next day, when the Rabbis took leave of him, he said: 'May the Rabbis go in peace.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a story about three Rabbis who had upset רב פפא. He dreams a פסוק about three shepherds being cut off and understands it is about them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in the dream pointed to the three Rabbis. רב פפא's goodbye, 'go in peace,' was a quiet hint that he would not see them again. The story shows how serious it is to cause pain to one's רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: They read to him (a פסוק shown in a dream)

phrases.english: They read to him in his dream:
"And I cut off the three shepherds."
phrases.notes: זכריה 11:8

phrases.english: The next day, when they were taking leave of him,
he said to them: May the Rabbis go in peace.
phrases.notes: He was hinting that this was the last time they would see each other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends a story that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב פפא understood from his dream that the three Rabbis would be cut off, and he parted from them with a hint of final farewell.

steps.title: רב שימי בר אשי stops challenging רב פפא
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי בר אשי often challenged רב פפא. He overheard רב פפא praying to be saved from embarrassment by him, so he chose to be silent from then on.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי בר אשי was often with רב פפא and challenged him a lot. One day he saw רב פפא bowing on his face in prayer and heard him say: 'May the Merciful One save us from the embarrassment of Shimi.' From then on רב שימי kept silent and did not challenge him anymore.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second, similar story about a student whose questions were causing his רבי pain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב שימי's questions were not wrong in themselves, but they were embarrassing רב פפא. Once he realized how much it hurt his teacher, he chose silence. This story balances the first one: here the student notices the pain and stops on his own.

keyTerms.meaning: Was often found before him (a regular student)
Fell on his face (bowing in prayer)

phrases.aramaic: רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי הֲוָה שְׁכִיחַ
phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Ashi was often found
before Rav Pappa,
and he would challenge him a great deal.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד חַזְיֵיהּ דִּנְפַל עַל אַפֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: One day he saw him fall on his face,
phrases.notes: Falling on his face is the bowing prayer said right after the תפילה.

phrases.english: he heard him say:
May the Merciful One save us from the embarrassment of Shimi.
He took silence upon himself,
and he did not challenge him anymore.

steps.whatToRemember: Both stories teach how careful a student must be not to cause pain or embarrassment to his רבי.
steps.triggerLanguage: רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי הֲוָה שְׁכִיחַ קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב פָּפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel story about a student and רב פפא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once רב שימי saw that his challenges embarrassed his רבי, he took on silence.

steps.title: ריש לקיש also holds that rain falls for an individual
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the topic of rain. It shows that ריש לקיש also holds rain can fall for one person, based on a פסוק in זכריה.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש also holds that rain can come for the sake of an individual. He said: From where do we know that rain comes for an individual? From the פסוק: 'Ask from ה' rain at the time of the late rain; ה' makes thunderclouds, and He will give them showers of rain, to a man, grass in the field.'
steps.whatsHappening: The stories are finished, and the גמרא goes back to the earlier question of whether rain can fall for one person. It brings ריש לקיש as another voice who agrees, and quotes his source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'וְאַף' (also) tells us this view was already mentioned earlier in the sugya, and now ריש לקיש is added as support for it. His source is a פסוק that ends with 'to a man,' which hints at one person. The next step will explain exactly how the פסוק teaches this.

keyTerms.meaning: And also (adding another opinion that agrees)
Rain for the sake of one individual
The late rain of the season

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish also holds
that rain can come for the sake of an individual,
as Reish Lakish said:
From where do we know that rain comes for an individual?
As it is written: "Ask from ה׳ rain at the time of the late rain;
phrases.notes: זכריה 10:1

phrases.english: ה׳ makes thunderclouds,
and He will give them showers of rain,
to a man, grass in the field."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ סָבַר מָטָר בִּשְׁבִיל יָחִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the stories and returns to the earlier discussion about rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ריש לקיש holds that rain can fall for the sake of one individual, based on זכריה 10:1.

steps.title: The word 'to a man' shows rain for one person
steps.stepSummary: One might think rain only falls for the whole people, so the פסוק says 'to a man' to show it can fall for one person.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think rain comes only for everyone together. So the פסוק says 'to a man.'
steps.whatsHappening: This explains how ריש לקיש reads the פסוק. The word 'לְאִישׁ' is the key word that teaches rain can come for one person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without that word, we would assume rain is only given to the whole community at once. 'לְאִישׁ' is singular, which narrows it to one individual.

keyTerms.meaning: Therefore the פסוק says (to teach otherwise)
To a man, to one person

phrases.english: One might think it is only for everyone together;
therefore the verse says "to a man."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains which word in ריש לקיש's פסוק teaches the rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word 'לְאִישׁ' teaches that rain can fall for one individual, not only for everyone together.

steps.title: A ברייתא narrows it to one field and one plant
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא continues reading the פסוק. 'Field' shows rain can fall for one field, and 'grass' shows it can fall for even one plant.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a ברייתא taught: If rain is 'to a man,' you might think it falls on all his fields. So the פסוק says 'field.' If it is 'field,' you might think it falls on the whole field. So the פסוק says 'grass.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that keeps reading the same פסוק, word by word, and narrows the idea further each time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word narrows the one before it: 'לְאִישׁ' means one man, 'שָׂדֶה' means just one of his fields, and 'עֵשֶׂב' means even one plant in that field. This shows how exact ה׳'s care can be when He sends rain.

phrases.english: And it was taught:
If it is "to a man," one might think it is for all his fields;
therefore the verse says: "field."
If it is "field," one might think it is for the whole field;
therefore the verse says: "grass."

steps.whatToRemember: From the פסוק 'לְאִישׁ עֵשֶׂב בַּשָּׂדֶה' we learn that rain can be sent for one person, for one of his fields, and even for one plant in it.
steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנְיָא: אִי לְאִישׁ, יָכוֹל לְכׇל שְׂדוֹתָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a ברייתא that carries ריש לקיש's reading further.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain can fall for a single field and even for a single plant.

steps.title: Rain fell only on the garden beds that needed it
steps.stepSummary: רב דניאל בר קטינא would check his garden every day, and rain fell only on the beds that needed water.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what happened with רב דניאל בר קטינא. He had a garden and checked it every day. He would say, 'This bed needs water, and this bed does not.' Then rain would come and water only the places that needed it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real-life story that shows the idea from step 5 actually happening: rain falling for one field, and even for one plant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 learned from the פסוק that rain can fall for a single field or a single plant. This story shows it in real life. The rain was so exact that it skipped the beds that did not need water.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּרַב דָּנִיאֵל בַּר קַטִּינָא
phrases.english: Like this case of רב דניאל בר קטינא
who had a certain garden.

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל יוֹמָא הֲוָה אָזֵיל וְסָיַיר לַהּ.
phrases.english: Every day he would go and check on it.
He would say: This bed needs water,
and this bed does not need water.
And rain would come and water
every place that needed water.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּרַב דָּנִיאֵל בַּר קַטִּינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real-life example of the ברייתא's teaching that rain can fall for one field or plant.
steps.raayaObject: Rain can fall for a single field or even a single plant.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of רב דניאל בר קטינא's garden.

steps.title: What does 'ה׳ עשה חזיזים' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the words 'ה׳ עשה חזיזים' mean in the same פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is meant by 'ה׳ makes חזיזים'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the פסוק in זכריה and asks about another phrase in it. This line sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps explained the words 'to a man,' 'field,' and 'grass.' Now the גמרא asks about a different phrase in the same פסוק, 'עשה חזיזים.'

keyTerms.meaning: A word in the פסוק about clouds that bring rain

phrases.english: What is 'ה׳ makes חזיזים'?
phrases.notes: זכריה 10:1, the same פסוק used in steps 3 to 5.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the story back to explaining another phrase of the פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the phrase 'ה׳ עשה חזיזים' teaches.

steps.title: Every צדיק gets his own cloud
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא says the plural 'חזיזים' teaches that הקב״ה makes a separate cloud for each צדיק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: This teaches that for every צדיק, הקב״ה makes a cloud just for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא answers the question: the פסוק says many clouds because each צדיק gets his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits the theme of rain for one person. It is not only that rain can fall for one person; הקב״ה makes a personal cloud for each צדיק.

phrases.english: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said:
This teaches that for every צדיק,
הקב״ה makes for him
a separate cloud of his own.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁכׇּל צַדִּיק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The plural 'חזיזים' teaches that each צדיק has his own cloud.

steps.title: What exactly are חזיזים? Flying clouds
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the word חזיזים actually means, and רב יהודה says: פורחות, flying clouds.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are חזיזים? רב יהודה said: flying clouds.
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא asks for the plain meaning of the word itself, and רב יהודה defines it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 explained what the word teaches. This step asks what kind of thing a חזיז is. רב יהודה says it is a 'flying' cloud, which the גמרא will explain soon.

phrases.english: What are 'חזיזים'?
רב יהודה said: Flying ones.
phrases.notes: He means flying clouds; the word 'clouds' is left out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the lesson of the word, asks for its plain meaning.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The plain meaning of the word חזיזים.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב יהודה: they are flying clouds.

steps.title: Flying clouds are a sign of rain
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that flying clouds are a sign that rain is coming.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Flying clouds are a sign that rain is coming.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן adds a teaching that matches רב יהודה: when you see flying clouds, rain is on the way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains why the פסוק links חזיזים with rain. Flying clouds are the clouds that come before rain.

phrases.english: רבי יוחנן said:
A sign of rain is flying clouds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב יהודה's definition by showing flying clouds go with rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Flying clouds signal that rain is coming.

steps.title: What is a flying cloud?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'flying clouds' are, and רב פפא says: a thin cloud under a thick cloud.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are flying clouds? רב פפא said: a thin cloud under a thick cloud.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a clear picture of a 'flying cloud,' and רב פפא describes it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The term 'פורחות' was still unclear. רב פפא makes it concrete: you see a thin, light cloud floating below a heavy, thick cloud.

phrases.english: What are flying clouds? רב פפא said:
A thin cloud under a thick cloud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the term used by רב יהודה and רבי יוחנן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What a flying cloud looks like.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A thin cloud below a thick cloud.
steps.whatToRemember: חזיזים = פורחות = flying clouds = a thin cloud under a thick one, and they are a sign of rain.

steps.title: Drizzle before rain or after rain
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says drizzle before rain means rain is coming, and drizzle after rain means the rain is stopping.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: Drizzle before rain means rain is coming. Drizzle after rain means the rain is stopping.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives another weather sign: light drizzle. What it tells you depends on when it falls.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same thing, drizzle, means two opposite things. Before rain it is the start of a storm. After rain it is the storm ending.

phrases.english: רב יהודה said:
Drizzle before rain: the rain is coming.
After rain: the rain is stopping.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: נְהִילָא מִקַּמֵּי מִיטְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another sign of rain after flying clouds.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Drizzle before rain signals rain; drizzle after rain signals the rain ending.

steps.title: Memory hooks: a sieve and goat droppings
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה repeats his two rules and gives a memory hook for each: a sieve for drizzle before rain, goat droppings for drizzle after rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Before rain, rain is coming; your memory hook is a sieve. After rain, rain is stopping; your memory hook is goat droppings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats רב יהודה's two rules. This time it adds a simple picture for each one so you will not mix them up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sieve drops a little flour before the real sifting starts, just like drizzle comes before heavy rain. A goat's droppings start big and end small, just like rain gets lighter at the end.
steps.confusionAlert: The words are repeated on purpose. This is not a new rule; each half of the rule now gets its own memory hook.

phrases.english: Before rain: the rain is coming.
And your memory hook: a sieve.
phrases.notes: A little flour falls through a sieve before you really start sifting, like drizzle before the real rain.

phrases.english: That after rain: the rain is stopping.
And your memory hook: goat droppings.
phrases.notes: A goat's droppings start large and end small, like rain that tapers off.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats רב יהודה's rule and attaches a memory hook to each half.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sieve = drizzle before rain means rain is coming; goat droppings = drizzle after rain means rain is ending.

steps.title: עולא sees flying clouds in בבל, but no rain comes
steps.stepSummary: עולא came to בבל, saw flying clouds and told people rain was coming, but it did not rain. He joked that Babylonian rain lies just like Babylonians do.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא came to בבל and saw flying clouds. He told the people: 'Clear away your things, because rain is coming now.' In the end, no rain came. He said: 'Just as the Babylonians lie, so their rains lie.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story where the sign of flying clouds did not work in בבל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא came from ארץ ישראל, where flying clouds reliably bring rain. In בבל the sign failed, so he made a sharp remark. The story shows that this sign is reliable in ארץ ישראל but not in בבל.
steps.whatToRemember: Flying clouds are a sign of rain, but עולא's story shows the sign did not hold true in בבל.

phrases.english: עולא came to בבל and saw flying clouds.
He said to them: Clear away your things,
because the rain is coming now.
In the end, the rain did not come.
He said: Just as the Babylonians lie,
so their rains lie.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows a case where the flying-cloud sign from רבי יוחנן did not work, in בבל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The flying-cloud sign did not hold true in בבל.

steps.title: עולא and the cheap dates of בבל
steps.stepSummary: עולא sees very cheap dates in בבל and wonders why Babylonians don't learn more. That night the dates hurt his stomach, and he changes his mind.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא came to בבל and saw a whole basket of dates selling for one זוז. He said: 'A basket of honey for a זוז, and the Babylonians still don't learn תורה?' That night the dates made him sick. He said: 'A basket of knives for a זוז, and still the Babylonians learn תורה!'
steps.whatsHappening: This is a second light story about עולא's visit to בבל. First he complains about the Babylonians, then he ends up praising them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first עולא thinks food is so cheap and sweet that Babylonians have every reason to sit and learn. After the dates hurt him, he sees them as 'knives.' Now he is impressed that Babylonians learn Torah despite their food.

keyTerms.meaning: a זוז, a small silver coin

phrases.english: עולא happened to come to בבל,
he saw a basket full of dates for one זוז.
He said: A basket full of honey for one זוז,
phrases.notes: By 'honey' he means the sweet dates. They taste like honey.

phrases.english: and the Babylonians do not busy themselves with Torah?
At night they hurt him,
phrases.notes: 'They' means the dates he ate.

phrases.english: he said: A basket full of knives for one זוז,
and still the Babylonians busy themselves with Torah!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story about עולא's visit to בבל, following his joke about Babylonian rain in step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עולא first criticizes the Babylonians for not learning despite cheap food, then praises them for learning despite food that hurts.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר: the world drinks from ocean water
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא brings רבי אליעזר's view that rain comes from the ocean, with a פסוק about a mist rising from the earth.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: רבי אליעזר says the whole world drinks from the ocean's water, as the פסוק says, 'A mist rose up from the earth and watered the whole face of the ground.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic: where does rain water come from? רבי אליעזר says it comes up from the ocean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר reads the פסוק literally. Water rises from below as a 'mist' and then waters the land. So the source of rain is the ocean down here.

phrases.english: It was taught in a ברייתא: רבי אליעזר says:
The entire world
drinks from the waters of the ocean,
as it says: 'And a mist went up from the earth
and watered the whole face of the ground.'
phrases.notes: בראשית 2:6

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, the source of rain, after the stories about עולא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain comes from ocean water that rises from the earth.

steps.title: But ocean water is salty
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע challenges רבי אליעזר: ocean water is salty, so how can it be rain?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע said to him: But ocean water is salty!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע attacks רבי אליעזר's idea with a simple fact about the world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rain water is sweet and drinkable, but ocean water is salty. If rain came from the ocean, it should be salty too.

phrases.english: רבי יהושע said to him:
But the ocean's waters are salty!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אליעזר's claim from step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אליעזר's claim that rain comes from the ocean.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Rain is sweet but ocean water is salty, so rain can't come from the ocean.

steps.title: The water becomes sweet in the clouds
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר answers that the ocean water turns sweet inside the clouds.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The water becomes sweet in the clouds.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר defends his view against the salt problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He agrees the ocean is salty. But the water changes on the way: by the time it falls as rain, the clouds have made it sweet.

phrases.english: He said to him: They become sweet in the clouds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יהושע's challenge from step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adds a missing stage: the water changes inside the clouds.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Ocean water would fall as salty rain.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clouds sweeten the ocean water before it falls.

steps.title: רבי יהושע: the world drinks from the upper waters
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע gives his own view: rain comes from waters up in the heavens.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע says: The whole world drinks from the upper waters, as the פסוק says, 'From the rain of the heavens it drinks water.'
steps.whatsHappening: Now the ברייתא gives רבי יהושע's own opinion, which is the opposite of רבי אליעזר's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע says rain does not come up from below at all. It comes from waters stored above. His פסוק says the land drinks 'from the rain of the heavens.'

keyTerms.meaning: the upper waters (waters above, in the heavens)

phrases.english: רבי יהושע says:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ מִמַּיִם הָעֶלְיוֹנִים הוּא שׁוֹתֶה,
phrases.english: The entire world drinks from the upper waters,
as it says: 'From the rain of the heavens it drinks water.'
phrases.notes: דברים 11:11

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to רבי אליעזר's in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain comes from the upper waters in the heavens.

steps.title: What about the mist that rises from the earth?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks how רבי יהושע explains the פסוק about a mist rising from the earth.
steps.simpleTranslation: But how do I explain the פסוק, 'And a mist went up from the earth'?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא challenges רבי יהושע with רבי אליעזר's פסוק. This sets up his explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: That פסוק sounds like water rises from below, which supports רבי אליעזר. If rain comes from above, what is this 'mist from the earth' about?

keyTerms.meaning: but how do I explain (fit in) this פסוק?

phrases.english: But how do I explain
'And a mist went up from the earth'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יהושע's view from step 19 using רבי אליעזר's פסוק from step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע's claim that rain comes only from above.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק says a mist rose from the earth to water the ground, which sounds like water comes from below.

steps.title: Clouds rise up to collect rain from above
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע explains that the 'mist from the earth' means clouds rise from below to the sky and fill up with rain water from above.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches that the clouds grow strong and rise up to the sky. They open their mouths like a leather bottle and take in rain water, as the פסוק says, 'They distill rain from His vapor.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers the challenge by reading the פסוק differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What rises from the earth is the clouds, not the water. The clouds go up empty, like an open bottle, and get filled with rain from the upper waters. So the פסוק fits his view.

phrases.english: It teaches that the clouds grow strong
and rise up to the sky,
and open their mouths like a leather bottle,
and take in rain water,
as it says: 'They distill rain from His vapor.'
phrases.notes: איוב 36:27

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereads the פסוק: the 'mist' rising from the earth is the clouds, not the water.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק means rain water comes up from the earth.
steps.terutzMaskana: Clouds rise from the earth and get filled with rain from above.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי יהושע is giving up and saying water comes from below. Only the clouds rise from the earth. The water still comes from above.

steps.title: Clouds are full of holes like a sieve
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא goes on: the clouds have holes like a sieve and sprinkle the water onto the ground.
steps.simpleTranslation: The clouds have holes like a sieve. They come and sprinkle water onto the ground, as the פסוק says, 'Sprinkling of water, thick clouds of the skies.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues describing how rain works, now explaining how the water comes down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After the clouds fill up, they don't dump the water all at once. They work like a sieve and let it out in small drops. The word חַשְׁרַת in the פסוק is read as 'sprinkling.'

keyTerms.meaning: sprinkle, let out little by little

phrases.english: And they have holes like a sieve,
phrases.notes: 'They' means the clouds.

phrases.aramaic: וּבָאוֹת וּמְחַשְּׁרוֹת מַיִם עַל גַּבֵּי קַרְקַע,
phrases.english: and they come and sprinkle water onto the ground,
as it says: 'Sprinkling of water, thick clouds of the skies.'
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 22:12

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the description from step 21: after the clouds fill up, this explains how the water comes down.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Clouds let out rain through tiny holes, like a sieve.

steps.title: A day of rain is as great as the day of creation
steps.stepSummary: The drops fall only a hair's width apart, which teaches that a rainy day is as great as the day heaven and earth were created.
steps.simpleTranslation: Between one drop and the next there is only a hair's width. This teaches you that a day of rain is as great as the day heaven and earth were created.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends its description of rain with a big lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The drops are extremely close together, only a hair apart, yet they come down as separate drops. This careful control shows how amazing rain is, so the ברייתא compares a rainy day to the day of creation.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי אליעזר: rain comes from the ocean and is sweetened in the clouds. רבי יהושע: rain comes from the upper waters; clouds rise to collect it and sprinkle it down like a sieve. Either way, a day of rain is as great as the day of creation.
steps.whyThisMatters: This lesson fits the theme of מסכת תענית: rain is a huge gift from ה׳, not something to take for granted.

phrases.english: And between one drop and the next drop there is nothing
except the width of a hair,
to teach you that a day of rain is as great
as the day on which heaven and earth were created.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the sieve description from step 22 and draws the lesson.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Rain comes down in perfectly separated drops, so a day of rain is as great as the day of creation.

steps.title: The verses that prove a rainy day is as great as Creation
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא brings פסוקים to show that rain is as wondrous as the creation of the world. Both use the phrase 'אין חקר', beyond searching out.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'Who does great things beyond searching out,' and right after that: 'Who gives rain upon the earth.' Later it says about ה׳ the Creator: 'There is no searching out His understanding.' And it also says: 'Who sets the mountains firm with His strength.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא is giving the source for what it just said: that a rainy day is as great as the day heaven and earth were created.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In איוב, rain is described as one of ה׳'s 'great things beyond searching out.' In ישעיהו, the same words 'אין חקר' describe ה׳ as the Creator of the world. Because the same phrase is used for both, rain is put on the same level as Creation. The last פסוק, about setting the mountains firm, comes from a chapter of תהילים that speaks about rain.

keyTerms.meaning: Beyond searching out; too great to fully understand
Later on, further along in the text

steps.whatToRemember: Rain and Creation are both called 'אין חקר', so a rainy day is as great as the day heaven and earth were created.

phrases.english: As it is said: "Who does great things beyond searching out,"
phrases.notes: איוב 5:9

phrases.english: and it is written: "Who gives rain upon the face of the earth,"
phrases.notes: איוב 5:10, the very next פסוק, so rain is one of those 'great things.'

phrases.english: and it is written further on:
"Have you not known? Have you not heard?
The everlasting God, ה׳,
there is no searching out His understanding."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 40:28. This פסוק is about ה׳ as Creator, and it uses the same words 'אין חקר.'

phrases.english: and it is written: "Who sets the mountains firm with His strength, etc."
phrases.notes: תהילים 65:7

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the verse-based proof for the claim in step 23.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that a rainy day is as great as the day of Creation.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The shared phrase 'אין חקר' in איוב 5:9-10 (rain) and ישעיהו 40:28 (Creation), with support from תהילים 65:7.

steps.title: Whose view fits 'He waters the mountains from His upper chambers'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which תנא's view matches the פסוק 'He waters the mountains from His upper chambers.' רבי יוחנן explains it as ה׳'s upper chambers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view matches the פסוק 'He waters the mountains from His upper chambers'? רבי יוחנן said this means from the upper chambers of הקב״ה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק and רבי יוחנן's reading of it. It asks which side of the argument about where rain comes from this reading supports.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן reads 'upper chambers' as the actual heavenly storehouses of ה׳, high above. That sounds like rain comes from above. So the גמרא wants to match it to one of the two views.

phrases.english: Whose view does this follow, that which is written:
"He waters the mountains from His upper chambers,"
phrases.notes: תהילים 104:13

phrases.english: and Rabbi Yochanan said:
from the upper chambers of the Holy One, Blessed be He.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ברייתא to checking a פסוק against the two views.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which view, רבי אליעזר's or רבי יהושע's, matches רבי יוחנן's reading of 'from His upper chambers'?

steps.title: It fits רבי יהושע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this reading matches רבי יהושע, who holds that rain comes from the waters above.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view? רבי יהושע's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question: water coming down from ה׳'s upper chambers fits רבי יהושע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע said in step 19 that rain comes from waters up in the heavens. ה׳'s 'upper chambers' fits that exactly. This sets up the next question: how would רבי אליעזר deal with this פסוק?

keyTerms.meaning: Like the view of רבי יהושע

phrases.english: Like whom? Like Rabbi Yehoshua.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The reading follows רבי יהושע, since rain comes from above.

steps.title: How רבי אליעזר reads 'from His upper chambers'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר holds that rain comes from the ocean below. He explains that the פסוק says 'from His upper chambers' because the clouds go up to the sky.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אליעזר? Since the clouds go up there, the פסוק calls the rain 'watering from His upper chambers.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how רבי אליעזר handles this פסוק, and right away gives his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is hidden in two words: 'and רבי אליעזר?' The problem is that the פסוק seems to say rain comes from above, against his view. His answer is that the water really comes from below. But the clouds carrying it rise high into the sky, so the פסוק can describe the rain as coming from above.

keyTerms.meaning: It calls them, it describes them as

phrases.english: And Rabbi Eliezer?
phrases.notes: Short for: how does רבי אליעזר explain this פסוק?

phrases.english: Since they go up there,
phrases.notes: 'They' are the clouds rising up toward the sky.

phrases.english: it calls them "waters from His upper chambers."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about and defends רבי אליעזר against the פסוק that fit רבי יהושע.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the פסוק as describing where the clouds are, not where the water comes from.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'From His upper chambers' means the water itself comes from above.
steps.terutzMaskana: The water comes from below. It is called 'from above' only because the clouds rise up there.

steps.title: Proof from 'dust from the heavens'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports רבי אליעזר's reading with a פסוק that speaks of 'powder and dust from the heavens.' There is no dust in heaven, so 'from the heavens' must mean it rose up there.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you don't say this, how do you explain 'powder and dust from the heavens'? Is there dust in heaven? Rather, since the dust rises up there, the פסוק calls it 'from the heavens.' So too, since the clouds go up there, it calls the rain 'from His upper chambers.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves that the תורה really talks this way. Something that goes up to the sky can be described as coming 'from the heavens.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dust obviously starts on the ground, yet the פסוק says it comes 'from the heavens.' That is only because it rises up there ('מִדְּלֵי לְהָתָם'). The same way of speaking explains 'from His upper chambers' for rain whose water started below.

keyTerms.meaning: For if you do not say so
How could you find such a case?
It is lifted up, it rises

steps.whatToRemember: רבי אליעזר: 'from His upper chambers' means the clouds rise up there, just like dust that rises is called 'from the heavens.'

phrases.english: For if you do not say so,
"powder and dust from the heavens"
phrases.notes: דברים 28:24

phrases.english: how could you find it?
phrases.notes: He means: there is no dust up in heaven, so how can dust come from there?

phrases.english: Rather, since it rises up there,
it calls it "from the heavens."
So too here: since they go up there,
it calls it "from His upper chambers."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the answer for רבי אליעזר in step 27 with a parallel פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the פסוק can say 'from above' about something that only rose up there.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 28:24, 'powder and dust from the heavens.'

steps.title: Whose view fits רבי חנינא's reading of 'He puts the depths in storehouses'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which view matches רבי חנינא. He reads the פסוק to mean that the deep waters are what fill the storehouses with grain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view matches what רבי חנינא said about the פסוק 'He gathers the waters of the sea like a heap; He puts the depths in storehouses'? What made the storehouses fill with grain? The depths.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second teaching and asks which side of the argument it fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא reads the end of the פסוק in a new way: the depths fill the storehouses. In other words, the deep waters water the crops and make the grain grow. That sounds like the water for the land comes from below.

phrases.aramaic: כְּמַאן אָזְלָא הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא:
phrases.english: Whose view does this follow, that which Rabbi Chanina said:
"He gathers the waters of the sea like a heap;
He puts the depths in storehouses."
phrases.notes: תהילים 33:7

phrases.english: What caused the storehouses to be filled with grain?
The depths.
phrases.notes: He reads the פסוק as saying the deep waters fill the storehouses, because they water the crops.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּמַאן אָזְלָא הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same 'whose view?' pattern as step 25, now with a teaching that leans the other way.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which view matches רבי חנינא's reading that the depths fill the storehouses?

steps.title: It fits רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא's reading matches רבי אליעזר, who holds that the world is watered from the ocean waters below.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like רבי אליעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי חנינא's teaching follows רבי אליעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the deep waters below are what make the grain grow, the water comes from below. That is רבי אליעזר's view, the opposite of the previous פסוק, which fit רבי יהושע.

keyTerms.meaning: Like the view of רבי אליעזר

phrases.english: Like Rabbi Eliezer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי חנינא's reading follows רבי אליעזר, since the water comes from the depths below.

steps.title: How does רבי יהושע read this פסוק?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבי יהושע explains the פסוק about the depths in storehouses. His answer begins with the word 'That' and continues on the next daf.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהושע? He would say: that פסוק...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the question around: now רבי יהושע has to explain a פסוק that seemed to fit רבי אליעזר. This step sets up his answer, which continues on the next daf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the same pattern as step 27, where רבי אליעזר had to explain a פסוק that fit רבי יהושע. Now רבי יהושע must show that 'He puts the depths in storehouses' does not mean that rain comes from below. His explanation starts with 'ההוא' and continues past this point.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehoshua?
phrases.notes: Short for: how does רבי יהושע explain this פסוק?

phrases.english: That...
phrases.notes: This is the first word of רבי יהושע's answer. It continues on the next daf.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יהושע with the reading that was just matched to רבי אליעזר.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע's view that rain comes from the waters above.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי חנינא reads the פסוק as saying the depths below fill the storehouses with grain. That suggests the water for the crops comes from below, against רבי יהושע.
